<!-- Figure 5: continuum vs. finite grid. Static SVG inlined verbatim from continuum_grid_figure.py. No interactivity: it is a conceptual sketch (the state-space continuum on the left, the finite Weyl-label plane on the right). The mini Bloch ball uses the same purity-gradient fill and latitude/longitude wireframe as Figures 3 and 4 (its gradient id is "purity-cg" to avoid colliding with the other inlined Bloch SVGs). The identity (0,0) is a grey dot on both sides. -->
<style>
.continuum-grid{max-width:680px;margin:1.25rem auto;}
.continuum-grid svg{width:100%;height:auto;display:block;}
.continuum-grid .cg-vh{position:absolute;width:1px;height:1px;padding:0;margin:-1px;overflow:hidden;clip:rect(0,0,0,0);border:0;}
</style>

<div class="continuum-grid">
  <p class="cg-vh">Two panels. On the left, a Bloch ball, the continuum of qubit states, shaded by purity with a latitude and longitude wireframe, carrying three coloured coordinate axes: X = (1,0) toward the lower left, Y = (1,1) to the right, Z = (0,1) upward, and a grey identity dot at the centre. On the right, the finite plane of Weyl labels: four points, the identity (0,0) drawn as a grey dot matching the ball centre, and the three nonzero points (1,0), (0,1), (1,1) in the matching axis colours, cycled by an example homomorphism h.</p>

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 680 300" font-family="Georgia, 'Times New Roman', serif" role="img" aria-label="Left: the continuum of qubit states with three coloured Bloch axes.
